evidence: placeOrder resolves products with requireProduct, builds the order with Order.place, and calls product.ensureAvailable and product.reserve. The domain objects enforce the rules; the service only orders the calls.
transition hands the lifecycle rules to order.advanceTo and coordinates product.dispatch across aggregates when the target is 'shipped'.
Persistence goes only through the injected ports OrderRepository and ProductRepository (orders.save, products.save, findById, findAll). There is no storage code in the file.
IDs and timestamps come from the injected IdGenerator and Clock ports, not from framework or system calls.
There is no HTTP, serialization or framework code; src/infrastructure/http.ts and server.ts are the files that use this service.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: OrderService does the job of an application layer. It coordinates use cases (place, get, list, transition, cancel). It loads aggregates through repository ports declared in the domain, hands state changes and invariants to domain methods (Order.place, advanceTo, cancel, Product.ensureAvailable, reserve, dispatch, release) and saves the results. It contains no persistence code, transport/HTTP handling or framework logic. The empty-items check is command input validation. Running a stock check across all lines before reserving any stock is a consistency step that spans several aggregates, which fits an application service. Dispatching stock when an order ships is also cross-aggregate coordination, and the domain methods decide the actual business rules. No ADR prose was given that would say otherwise.
